topics.title: EEG topoplot practice, statistical foundations, and the uncertainty gap
topics.research_question: What evidence motivates uncertainty-aware EEG topoplots, and what is still unknown?
topics.scope_note: This page links practice surveys, ERP benchmark/statistical methods, and scalp interpolation. It does not claim that any reviewed encoding has been validated specifically for uncertainty topoplots.

rows.note: Direct evidence that adding uncertainty is a practical ERP-tooling problem.
Shows omission and incomplete awareness among surveyed practitioners.
Different interpretations of topoplot time series imply that uncertainty semantics must be explicit.
Provides a concrete ERP convention for waveform uncertainty, while not solving spatial-map uncertainty.
Supplies benchmark variability and noise that could support method testing.
Shows that trial-level variability can be retained statistically before visualization.
Provides an early map-level smoothing and confidence-interval foundation.
Broader neuroscience evidence that uncertainty is frequently omitted or unlabeled.

gaps: No archived study directly compares uncertainty encodings on EEG scalp topographies using perceptual or decision tasks.

The literature does not establish whether viewers interpret uncertainty as measurement noise, between-participant variability, model uncertainty, interpolation uncertainty, or statistical confidence unless the display states it.
Topoplot interpolation creates spatial smoothness between electrodes, but the reviewed user studies do not test how that smoothness interacts with an uncertainty overlay.
No evidence matrix row establishes which encoding best preserves sign, magnitude, spatial pattern, and uncertainty simultaneously for EEG audiences.

topics.title: Why scientific visualizations omit uncertainty
topics.research_question: How common is uncertainty omission, and what explanations are supported?
topics.scope_note: Audits estimate omission only within their sampled disciplines and dates; qualitative studies explain rationales but not their population prevalence.

rows.note: Neuroscience figure audit documents omission and missing labels.
ERP-practitioner survey documents omitted error bars and awareness gaps.
Map review documents a large text/caption/map integration gap.
Ecosystem audit shows incomplete reporting across multiple uncertainty sources.
Clinical figure audit identifies omitted uncertainty as an interpretive risk.
Qualitative evidence supplies audience, workflow, convention, and signal-obfuscation rationales.
Industrial case expands causes to metadata and organizational infrastructure.

gaps: Audits use different definitions and denominators, so their percentages should not be pooled.
Evidence is largely cross-sectional; causal tests of whether improved software defaults reduce omission are scarce.
Omission rates specific to published EEG topoplots have not been directly audited in the archived collection.
The consequences of omission for EEG interpretation and downstream decisions remain unquantified.

topics.title: Integrated versus separate value–uncertainty displays
topics.research_question: When should value and uncertainty be integrated in one display rather than separated?
topics.scope_note: The evidence is mixed because studies use different tasks, maps, encodings, and audiences. Treat apparent disagreement as task dependence, not as a simple contradiction.

rows.note: Superposition outperformed juxtaposition for a targeted value-plus-uncertainty identification task.
Authors recommend integration or interaction when information fusion is required.
Separate maps were more accurate but slower than a combined whitening map.
Review finds adjacent maps may aid uncertainty retrieval while other outcomes differ by task.
Medical-imaging survey flags correspondence costs for separate uncertainty images.
Illustrative argument that bivariate maps reveal joint spatial patterns.
The same paper acknowledges increased interpretation difficulty.
Early experiments show large elementary-reading and legend-learning costs for bivariate maps.
Multi-symbol effectiveness varied by uncertainty condition and symbol family.
Integration performance changes with practice and transfers across display families.

gaps: No direct comparison exists for separate versus integrated uncertainty in EEG topoplots.
Studies rarely separate costs of legend learning from costs of spatial correspondence and visual crowding.
The optimal design may differ for lookup, spatial-pattern detection, comparison, and decision tasks; EEG-specific priorities remain to be defined.
Interactive linking between a topoplot and a separate uncertainty view is suggested by prior work but not tested here.

topics.title: Bivariate colour-map origins, readability, and later quality work
topics.research_question: What does the reviewed literature establish about the origins, readability, and later assessment of bivariate colour maps?
topics.scope_note: The sources cover different map classes and methods. Meyer documents Census development, Wainer tests the resulting two-variable maps, Strode addresses bivariate choropleth design, and Bernard assesses multivariate 2D colormaps while explicitly excluding bivariate metric maps. These records form a historical sequence, not one directly comparable experiment series.

rows.note: Primary documentation dates the Bureau's cross-map proposal to 1974 and its publication to 1975.
The intended relational-reading benefit is an author interpretation, not a measured outcome.
The source states that reader evaluation was still underway.
Controlled elementary-reading trials found a threefold mean error rate despite slightly faster bivariate responses.
Removing the legend produced severe bivariate performance degradation.
Later work structures bivariate choropleth palettes around the relationship and reader question.
Task-based quality assessment is relevant by analogy but was not applied to bivariate metric maps.

gaps: Olson's 1981 paper is cited by the manuscript but is not archived in the project, so it does not yet have a claim-level ingestion record.
Meyer reports design rationale and ongoing research rather than reader-performance results.
Wainer's small student sample, historic palettes, and elementary lookup tasks do not establish performance for modern bivariate uncertainty maps.
Bernard's task-based assessment cannot be cited as a direct evaluation of bivariate metric maps because that class was explicitly excluded.

topics.title: Task and audience dependence of uncertainty encodings
topics.research_question: Is there a generally best uncertainty visualization, or does performance depend on task and audience?
topics.scope_note: Across domains, evidence strongly favors conditional conclusions. This is a synthesis across heterogeneous settings, not a pooled meta-analysis.

rows.note: Technique performance changed with task and dimensionality.
Continuous versus binned encoding showed a task-dependent speed–accuracy tradeoff.
Separate and combined maps traded speed against accuracy.
Authors explicitly reject a universal metaphor after three perceptual studies.
Systematic review recommends task-centered evaluation.
HOP advantage was large for multi-quantity ordering but not universal for one-variable questions.
Handbook synthesis distinguishes compact expert encodings from more intuitive lay formats.
Computational assessment operationalizes task-specific palette selection.
Six temporal encodings traded performance across boundary, duration, and probability tasks.
Non-expert preference and behavioral performance diverged.
Preference rankings alone do not establish decision effectiveness.
Recent scoping review warns against treating preference as performance.

gaps: EEG-domain tasks need explicit definition: amplitude lookup, sign detection, spatial extent, peak localization, condition comparison, and inference are not interchangeable.
Expertise and statistical literacy are inconsistently measured across existing studies.
Few studies test accessibility, color-vision diversity, or small-multiple publication constraints together with uncertainty comprehension.
Performance, preference, confidence, and scientific validity can diverge and should not be collapsed into one outcome.

topics.title: Sample-based and image-distribution approaches
topics.research_question: What does the literature establish about showing repeated possible outcomes rather than only intervals?
topics.scope_note: HOPs and quantile dotplots have direct behavioral evidence in this collection; distribution-over-images is a general mathematical framework. None has been evaluated on EEG topoplots here.

rows.note: Direct experimental evidence for improved multi-quantity ordering judgments.
The animated condition took somewhat longer, though not significantly overall.
Authors connect performance to counting and integration of sampled outcomes.
Generalizes sampled rendering to arbitrary statistical graphics.
Provides formal coverage arguments under stated assumptions.
Review cautions that animation has not generally outperformed static uncertainty displays.
HOPs lowered evidence thresholds in a noisy-trend discrimination task.
Order and practice affected performance.
Quantile dotplots supported near-optimal transit decisions after repeated trials.

gaps: No study tests animated or aggregated sampled topoplots for spatial-pattern, peak, or condition-comparison tasks.
Animation duration, sample count, temporal dependence, and accessibility need EEG-specific evaluation.
Image aggregation can mix color and intensity in ways that may obscure signed EEG values.
Coverage guarantees do not establish perceptual calibration or correct scientific interpretation.

topics.title: How to evaluate and report an uncertainty-topoplot study
topics.research_question: What methodological evidence should guide evaluation and reporting of a new uncertainty-topoplot design?
topics.scope_note: This matrix concerns study design and reporting, not the choice of a final encoding.

rows.note: Start from evaluation goal and research question before choosing method.
Use task-centered evaluation and report expertise and context.
For applied work, ground abstraction and alternatives in a real domain problem.
ERP CORE offers reproducible tasks, data, and pipelines for testing.
Benchmark noise distributions can support stimulus construction and quality checks.
Incomplete uncertainty reporting shows why source-specific reporting criteria matter.
Published figure conventions can be audited systematically rather than assumed.
Evaluation should extend beyond constrained accuracy to explanation and downstream decisions.
Recent geospatial evidence remains heterogeneous and thin on direct comparisons.
Learning curves matter when evaluating a novel display.
Include diagnostic tasks sensitive to known encoding-induced biases.

gaps: A preregistered EEG-specific task taxonomy for uncertainty topoplots is absent.
Future studies should report exclusions, denominators, stimuli, interpolation, reference, uncertainty definition, colormap, display size, and participant EEG/statistical expertise.
Accuracy, response time, confidence, preference, calibration, and scientific decision quality should be analyzed as distinct outcomes.
Open stimuli and code are needed to compare new encodings with conventional topoplots and separate uncertainty panels.

topics.title: Statistical interpretation and audit foundations
topics.research_question: What checks help align statistical code, study design, and reported scientific claims?
topics.scope_note: Gelman, Hill, and Vehtari provide methodological framing, while EEG and reporting sources provide domain context. This matrix is an audit guide, not evidence that a particular project implementation is correct.

rows.note: Check whether calculations omit important sampling, measurement, or model uncertainty.
Check for significant/nonsignificant dichotomies that overstate differences.
Check whether conditional associations are mislabeled as causal effects.
Check fitted models against observed data and replicated predictions.
Check whether the analysis preserves or discards trial-level variability consistently with the research question.
Check whether measurement noise and participant variation are defined and reported rather than conflated.
Incomplete source-specific uncertainty reporting motivates an explicit reporting checklist.

gaps: A project audit still requires reading the actual analysis code, data transformations, model objects, and manuscript claims; handbook principles cannot substitute for execution checks.
The archived sources do not define one universally correct EEG topoplot uncertainty model.
Simulation-based calibration, sensitivity analysis, and validation targets must be chosen for the actual estimand and study design.
Every reported number should be traceable from manuscript text to generated output and the code/data state that produced it.
